title: Hospitality
lead: Welcoming strangers with food, shelter and protection was a sacred duty in the ancient Near East and remains one in the Bible's ethics. Abraham's welcome of three visitors (Genesis 18) became the model, and the New Testament asks believers to love strangers and open their homes (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2).

sections.b: The Law commands Israel to love the foreigner, "because you were foreigners in the land of Egypt" (Leviticus 19:33–34). Hospitality saves and its violation horrifies: Rahab hides the spies (Joshua 2), the widow of Zarephath feeds Elijah (1 Kings 17:8–16), and the Levite's concubine is handed to a mob in a town that refused to take strangers in (Judges 19). Job swears his door was always open to the traveler (Job 31:32). Jesus is a guest at many tables (Luke 10:38–42; 19:1–10), tells hosts to invite those who cannot repay (Luke 14:12–14), and says that whoever welcomes a stranger welcomes him (Matthew 25:35). The letters make it a mark of church life and leadership (Romans 12:13; 1 Timothy 3:2; 1 Peter 4:9; 3 John 5–8).
